schools.summary: Clarke (with Calmet) and Wesley date 'that day' after the dedication, on Nehemiah's return from the Persian court in the thirty-second year, when abuses had crept in.
Gill: 'on that day' cannot mean the dedication itself, for so quick a corruption is unthinkable; it falls after twelve years' rule and a journey to Babylon.
Henry makes the public reading the lesson — the word discovers sin and works the will to separate from it, as the mixed multitude (Num. 11:4; Deut. 23:3) was here put away.

debates.question: What does the law barring Ammon and Moab from 'the congregation' forbid?

sides.position: Only matrimonial alliance — 'this, and this alone, is the meaning of the law'
Incorporation and settlement in the commonwealth, as well as marriage

themes: the public reading of the law

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch supply the ground: Ammon and Moab met not Israel with bread, hired Balaam to curse, but God turned the curse to blessing; the date stays indefinite amid frequent readings.
Henry presses the aggravation — unprovoked malice repaid to a people forbidden to harm them, so that those who met not Israel with bread were justly barred from the congregation.
Gill treats the verse as the compressed echo of the fuller Balaam narrative.

themes: the ancient enmity of Ammon and Moab
Balaam's hired curse turned to blessing
righteousness, not spite, bars the door

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch trace 'mixed multitude' to the word of Exod. 12:38, here the resident foreigners of various nations, all separated once the law was understood; the date cannot be fixed.
Clarke reads the purge of strange women and children of illegal unions; Wesley of all the heathen peoples they had allied with.
Gill: the law heard forbade marriage with Ammon, Moab, and the rest, and bred immediate compliance.

debates.question: Who were the 'mixed multitude' that were separated?

sides.position: The foreign wives and the children born of the mixed marriages
The heathen peoples they had contracted alliance with
Resident foreigners of various nations dwelling among Israel

themes: the power of the word to separate

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott take Eliashib to be the high priest, inferring it from his oversight of the temple chambers; Ellicott notes his suspicious absence from the preceding festivities.
Clarke doubts whether this was the high priest but grants no evidence against it, tracing the alliance through the grandson's marriage to Sanballat's daughter; Wesley names him the high priest.
Gill sets the corruption 'before' the law was read and acted upon.

debates.question: Is this Eliashib the high priest?

sides.position: Yes — the high priest, whose office gave him control of the chamber
Possibly a different priest, though there is no certain evidence either way

themes: the priest set over the chambers
an Ammonite in the temple courts

schools.summary: Gill and Ellicott note the great chamber made by throwing several into one; Keil and Delitzsch list the holy stores it had held — offerings, frankincense, vessels, tithes for Levites, singers, porters.
Wesley: the sacred things were removed and the rooms furnished to lodge Tobiah for freer communication with him.
Henry pours out indignation on four counts, calling it next to setting up an idol, and a corrupting of the covenant of Levi (Mal. 2:8).

themes: the great chamber made of many

schools.summary: Clarke lays out the chronology — twelve years, then a year at Babylon, then leave to return; Wesley: Eliashib seized the occasion of the governor's absence.
Henry makes the absence a proverb of vigilance — the enemy sows tares while the servants sleep (Matt. 13:25), the golden calf was made while Moses was in the mount (Exod. 32:1).
Ellicott reads the verse as a parenthesis and explains 'king of Babylon' by the court's location where Nehemiah rejoined the king.
Gill: had Nehemiah been present, these things would never have been suffered.
Keil and Delitzsch fix the charge twice named — 'the evil that Eliashib did for Tobiah' — laying the blame on the host, not the intruder, and stressing the profanation reached the temple courts.
Gill notes Nehemiah returned with the king's leave and commission, clothed again with authority to act.
Henry marks the grief of a good governor to see the chief priest betray the cause he should have guarded.

Keil and Delitzsch read the whole sweep — furniture flung out, chamber purified, holy vessels restored — and infer from 'household stuff' that Tobiah had dwelt there; Ellicott marks Nehemiah's emotion at a priestly desecration.
Clarke likens the deed to Christ cleansing the temple (Matt. 21:12); Wesley lists the aggravations — a stranger, an Ammonite, admitted by the high priest himself.
Gill grounds the grief in a sacred place turned to the common use of a heathen enemy.
Keil and Delitzsch have the vessels, meat offering, and frankincense restored to the cleansed rooms; Ellicott marks the accuracy that the tithes are not yet brought back, the next verses showing why.
Gill takes the ceremonial uncleanness from a heathen's habitation to require the water of separation (Num. 19:9), not mere washing.
Henry reads the sequence — cast out, cleanse, then furnish — as a figure of repentance, the heart purged before it is filled with the Spirit's graces.
Keil and Delitzsch explain the daily portions discontinued, forcing the Levites to their fields; Ellicott ties those fields to the Levitical cities (Num. 35:2).
Wesley offers alternative culprits — the corrupt priest or the covetous people; Clarke blames the negligent rulers who permitted the abuses.
Henry: God's house is the Levite's place, not his field; and a scandalous maintenance makes a scandalous ministry, the work neglected because the workmen are.
Gill: the tithes were diverted or withheld, and the unpaid Levites deserted their station.

debates.question: Who was chiefly to blame that the Levites went unpaid?

sides.position: The corrupt priest Eliashib, or the covetous people, diverting or withholding the tithes
The negligent rulers who permitted the abuse
The Levites themselves, non-resident in their fields, and the people who forsook them

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch make the seganim responsible for the dues and have Nehemiah gather the Levites back to their place; Ellicott marks the rich men's abuse of his absence and the broken covenant.
Clarke shows Nehemiah using the people's own covenant words (Neh. 10:39) as reproof; Wesley charges the priests with neglect and breach of promise.
Henry lays the fault on the rulers, and notes the careless would do better if only called upon.
Gill takes the rulers to be the priests set over the chambers.

debates.question: Who were the 'rulers' Nehemiah contended with?

sides.position: The priests set over the chambers
The seganim, heads of the community
The covetous rich who exploited his absence

themes: 'Why is the house of God forsaken?'
the Levites restored to their places

schools.summary: Gill: seeing a right use now made of the tithes, and the proper persons reinstated, the people brought their dues again.
Wesley: they gave out of respect to Nehemiah and confidence the tithes would be rightly applied.
Keil and Delitzsch set the renewed giving in the covenant obligation the people had taken and lately broken.
Henry: Nehemiah's zeal provoked theirs — the better church-work is done, the better church-dues are paid.
Clarke: they were reported trustworthy, steady while others grew careless; Wesley: chosen faithful by common consent, sought the more diligently after the former trustees' perfidy.
Ellicott sees the reform made effectual by organization — a balanced board of priest, scribe, Levite, and a lay under-steward, all faithful men.
Gill: new treasurers, the former officers being dead or unfaithful.
Henry: tried then trusted, a good degree purchased (1 Tim. 3:13), their office to receive and to distribute.
Keil and Delitzsch take the petition as committing his labour for the sanctuary to God's remembrance; Ellicott hears the faithful servant begging a merciful remembrance.
Clarke: were God strict to mark amiss, even good deeds must be wiped out — so Nehemiah casts himself on mercy, not merit.
Henry marks the modesty — 'Remember me,' not 'Reward me' — trusting God not to be unrighteous to forget (Heb. 6:10), who does more than we ask.
Gill: he asks not in strict justice but in grace, that God accept the work done for his name.

themes: God does more than we ask

schools.summary: Henry makes the verse a remonstrance — the presses trod, the asses laden, against Exod. 34:21, Deut. 5:14, Jer. 17:21 — and grounds the whole: religion is never in the throne while sabbaths are trodden under foot.
Ellicott marks the profanation most determined in the country and reaching into Jerusalem.
Clarke sees the sabbath totally disregarded.
Gill: treading the press was no work of necessity, but might have been deferred.

themes: sabbath profaned in field and city
needless labour on the holy day
religion decays as the sabbath falls

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch argue the verb means to tarry, not settle; Ellicott takes the Tyrians (who once brought temple timber, Ezra 3:7) to have formed a colony supplying fish — the offence being the sabbath sale in Jerusalem.
Gill: they dwelt there, bringing fish up from Joppa, with lodgings by the fish gate.
Wesley: done in the holy city, in manifest contempt of God and man.

debates.question: Did the men of Tyre settle in Jerusalem or merely tarry to trade?

sides.position: A resident colony, with lodgings by the fish gate
Not settlers but sojourners, tarrying only to sell

themes: sabbath merchandise in the holy city

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch have Nehemiah remind the nobles that such acts brought exile and oppression on the fathers; Ellicott: the appeal supposes their knowledge of Jeremiah's warning and its fulfilment (Jer. 17:27).
Clarke: the evils came through the nobles' negligence, which Nehemiah proved to their faces; Wesley: the sin fell on them by connivance and example.
Henry: the greatest are not too high to be reproved, and are to be contended with first; connivance makes the magistrate guilty who bears the sword in vain.
Gill takes the nobles for the civil magistrates, sharply reproved for neglect of duty.
Keil and Delitzsch: the fathers by such acts drew down 'all this evil,' the exile and present servitude, and the living only add to the wrath already resting on Israel.
Henry sets out the reasoning — sabbath-breaking was among the sins that brought the judgments, and to repeat it invites them again, as Ezra warned (Ezra 9:14).
Gill reads the parallel simply: did not your fathers profane the sabbath in like manner?

themes: the exile as a moral verdict

schools.summary: Clarke: after sunset Friday he shut the gates and set his own servants to watch, not trusting the ordinary officers; Wesley marks the same diffidence in the common gatekeepers.
Gill, with Jarchi, reads 'began to be dark' of the sabbath-eve shadows stretched over the gates before sunset.
Ellicott: the servants were used provisionally until the Levitical guard was appointed (Neh. 13:22).
Henry: he aimed at reformation, guarding the day's edges, admitting worshippers but barring sellers.

themes: shutting the gates before the sabbath

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch: since egress could not be refused the inhabitants, the sabbath was broken outside the gates, so Nehemiah moved to end the evasion; Ellicott: the traders' return exposed their intent.
Gill pictures the Tyrians camping outside, hoping buyers would come out to them.
Henry: they lay before the walls wishing the sabbath gone, the world pressing hard against the fence of the commandment.

themes: the world pressing at the fence

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch: 'I will lay hands on you' means drive you away by force, and from that time they came no more.
Clarke reads the threat as imprisonment — 'I will imprison every man of you' — which had the desired effect.
Gill hears a solemn protest, a calling of heaven and earth to witness.
Henry: resolute reformers accomplish more than they imagine — vice made cowardly when the magistrate becomes a terror to it.

themes: the abuse ended at a word
a magistrate willing to be feared

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch own the brevity of the notice but take the Levites, purified, to be set as the standing sabbath guard; Ellicott reads the cleansing as for a sacred duty, with reference to their past neglect.
Wesley explains the double propriety of cleansing for a holy work on a holy day; Clarke defends Nehemiah, the added 'spare me' proving he leaned wholly on mercy.
Gill: the Levites cleansed from ceremonial uncleanness, fit to serve on the sabbath.
Henry balances 'Remember me' (Ps. 40:5) with 'spare me' — the best saints in their best acts need sparing mercy, pleading God's greatness, not their merit.

outliers.note: Turns the added 'spare me according to thy mercy' into a defence of Nehemiah against those who brand him a mere self-righteous worker, insisting he expected nothing but through God's mercy.

themes: Levites set to keep the gates

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch read 'saw' as 'visited,' and infer from the children's speech that the intermarried dwelt on the borders; Ellicott judges these exceptional but flagrant cases.
Henry sees the cast-out sin re-entering after Ezra's reform (Ezra 9), the covenant profaned as Malachi charged (Mal. 2:11), a good governor healing the streams by the spring.
Gill: Ashdod a Philistine city and mart of the Arabians, a snare, while unions with Ammon and Moab were flatly unlawful.
Keil and Delitzsch: half the children spoke Ashdodite and could not speak the Jews' language; Ellicott takes it for a single mixture of Philistine and Aramaic.
Clarke argues for children of different mothers in one house, each set speaking a whole tongue, not a single jargon.
Gill offers a mixed tongue, or 'half' as the number of children chiefly bred by their mothers.
Henry: children learn their mothers' speech — reason enough against the unequal yoke and for governing children's tongues.

debates.question: What does 'half in the speech of Ashdod' mean?

sides.position: Half the children — those bred by foreign mothers — spoke wholly the foreign tongue
Every child spoke a single mongrel dialect, a mixture of Philistine and Hebrew

themes: losing the mother tongue of the covenant
the peril of the unequal yoke

schools.summary: Wesley reads 'cursed' as excommunication and the stripes and shaving as legal, disgraceful penalties (Deut. 25:2); Clarke as a denouncing of God's judgments and the law's sentence.
Ellicott takes 'cursed' as echoing the covenant sanction the people swore (Neh. 10:29-30), and contrasts Ezra plucking his own hair (Ezra 9:3).
Henry makes the contrast the key — Ezra plucked his own hair in sorrow, Nehemiah plucked theirs in indignation, both graces of one Spirit — the oath binding them against relapse.
Gill takes the contending as argument, admonition, and sharp reproof.

debates.question: What does it mean that Nehemiah 'cursed them'?

sides.position: Excommunication — cast out of the society of God's people
A denouncing of God's judgments and the sentence of the law
Echoing the covenant sanction the people had sworn on themselves

themes: Ezra's own hair versus the offenders'

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch trace the ascending honours — peerless, beloved, king over all Israel — that made Solomon's fall so terrible; Ellicott marks the shrewd appeal to a history the offenders knew and revered.
Henry: Solomon's wisdom could not secure him, his favour was forfeited, his kingdom rent — let him that stands take heed lest he fall on so plain a precipice.
Gill: Solomon sinned by these very things, drawn into idolatry by strange wives (1 Kings 11).

themes: let him that stands take heed

schools.summary: Henry: an iniquity the judge could not connive at — the plea to keep the wives refused, for there was no other remedy against the guilt and infection — the sin shown in the glass of the commandment (Deut. 7:3).
Clarke: if God spared not the beloved Solomon, shall we spare you who bring down his judgments?
Gill: shall we suffer it, connive at it, and not punish for it?

themes: no conniving at a great evil
the plea to keep the wives refused
sin shown in the glass of the commandment

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch supply the unstated reason — the son-in-law of Sanballat would not dismiss his wife, so Nehemiah drove him off; Ellicott marks the doubly scandalous alliance and the exile.
Clarke names him Manasseh, struck off the priestly list; Wesley (with Josephus) traces the rival Samaritan temple on Gerizim that he built by Sanballat's interest.
Gill identifies the grandson of the high priest, taken by Josephus for Manasseh, brother of Jaddua.
Henry sees the seed of the Samaritan schism lasting to the Lord's day (John 4:20), discipline sparing not even the high priest's own kin.

themes: the origin of the Samaritan schism

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch treat the prayer as the turn to the concluding summary; Ellicott commits the priestly violation to God alone and explains the covenant of the priesthood (Lev. 21:6).
Clarke: God will remember and punish, the words understood declaratively — announcing rather than merely wishing the judgment.
Henry uniquely opens the gentler sense — a prayer for their conviction and conversion — or else a prophecy that God would remember the sin against them.
Gill reads it plainly as an imprecation — remember them, to punish, for defiling the priesthood.

debates.question: Is 'Remember them, O my God' an imprecation or a plea for their conversion?

sides.position: A prayer that God punish the defilers of the priesthood
Possibly a prayer for their conviction and conversion

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch read the concluding recapitulation — cleansed from heathen customs and marriages, the wards of priests and Levites appointed to their offices; Ellicott adds a likely formal service of expiation.
Gill: both people and priests purged from the strange wives, made to put them away or flee.
Henry sees the aim of his whole government — not to enrich himself but to purify a peculiar people and set every priest in his business.

themes: the courses of priests and Levites restored

schools.summary: Clarke calls the wood-offering a most necessary regulation (Neh. 10:34) and reads 'Remember me for good' as 'have mercy upon me,' closing with a tribute to Nehemiah the patriot; Wesley makes 'for good' the summary of all our petitions.
Ellicott marks the solemn close — Nehemiah committing his contested reformation to the Righteous Judge — and notes these words end the annals of Old Testament history.
Gill: Levites appointed to receive and store the wood brought at the fixed times, and to carry it to the altar.
Henry: public service is often forgotten by men (Eccl. 9:15), so Nehemiah takes God for his paymaster, resting his work on divine remembrance.

themes: 'Remember me, O my God, for good'
the end of Old Testament history
Nehemiah the patriot resting on grace
